passages.title: Gauge numbers run backwards
passages.text:
Sheet metal thickness is given as a gauge number, and the scale runs opposite to
the way most people expect: the larger the gauge number, the thinner the metal.
Sixteen gauge is thicker than twenty gauge, and twenty-four gauge is thinner
still. The convention survives from a time when sheet was produced by drawing it
through successive dies, and the number recorded how many passes the metal had
been through. More passes meant thinner stock, so a higher count came to mean a
lighter sheet.

The practical consequence is that gauge numbers cannot be compared across
materials. A gauge number refers to a weight per unit area, not a distance, and
because steel, aluminum and copper differ in density, the same gauge number
corresponds to a different thickness in each. Sixteen gauge aluminum is
noticeably thicker than sixteen gauge steel, because it takes more aluminum by
volume to reach the same weight. Anyone ordering by gauge alone, without naming
the material, has not specified the job.

For that reason many specifications now give a decimal thickness alongside the
gauge, or in place of it. A drawing that calls for 0.0598 inch steel leaves
nothing to interpret, while one that calls for sixteen gauge relies on the
reader knowing which gauge table applies. Where both appear and they disagree,
the decimal governs, because it is the measurement that can be checked directly
with a micrometer on the material in hand.

The habit of checking rather than assuming matters most on repair work, where
the existing material was ordered under a table that may no longer be the one in
use. Measuring the old sheet takes a moment and settles the question. Ordering
from the gauge number stamped on a decades-old drawing, without measuring, is
how a job ends up with stock that looks right on paper and is wrong on the
bench.

passages.title: Why torque is specified
passages.text:
A bolted joint does not hold because the bolt is strong. It holds because the
bolt has been stretched, and the tension in that stretched bolt clamps the parts
together. Tightening a nut is a way of stretching the bolt, and the torque
figure in a specification is an indirect way of aiming at a particular stretch.
It is indirect because most of the effort applied at the wrench never reaches
the bolt as tension at all.

Of the torque applied, a large share is consumed by friction under the nut face
and in the threads. Only the remainder does the useful work of stretching the
fastener. The exact split depends on the condition of the parts, which is why
the same torque figure produces different clamping forces on a dry joint, an
oiled joint and a joint with a plated fastener. A specification that names a
torque without naming the lubrication condition has left out something that
changes the result substantially.

Under-tightening and over-tightening fail in different ways, and the difference
matters when a joint is being diagnosed. A joint that is too loose allows the
parts to move against each other under load, and that movement, repeated, works
the fastener loose or fatigues it until it breaks. A joint that is too tight may
yield the bolt on assembly, so that it no longer springs back and the clamping
force falls away. The loose joint usually announces itself gradually; the
over-tightened one may have already lost its clamp before the assembly leaves
the bench.

This is why a torque wrench is checked against a standard periodically rather
than trusted indefinitely, and why a fastener that has been tightened past yield
is replaced rather than re-used. Neither precaution is about the strength of the
bolt. Both are about preserving the stretch that does the actual holding.

passages.title: Balancing an air system
passages.text:
A duct system that has been installed exactly to drawing will still not deliver
the airflow the drawing intended. Fittings, joints and bends each add resistance
that the design accounted for only approximately, and the fan responds to the
total resistance it actually meets rather than the one that was calculated.
Balancing is the work of correcting that difference after the fact, by measuring
what each outlet actually delivers and adjusting dampers until the distribution
matches the design.

The order in which the work is done matters more than the individual
adjustments. Closing a damper at one outlet does not simply reduce the air at
that outlet; it raises the resistance of that branch, which sends more air to
every other outlet on the system. Balancing one outlet at a time and moving on
therefore undoes earlier work continuously. The usual method is to find the
outlet that is furthest below its target, treat it as the reference, and set the
others relative to it, accepting that several passes will be needed before the
readings settle.

Measurement introduces its own difficulty. Air leaving a diffuser is turbulent,
and a reading taken too close to the face or off to one side will not represent
the flow. Readings are taken at a consistent distance and position, and repeated,
because a single reading in a turbulent stream says very little. Where readings
disagree from one pass to the next by more than a small margin, the usual cause
is the measurement position rather than a change in the system.

None of this is a sign that the design was wrong. A design predicts; a system
behaves. Balancing is the step that reconciles the two, and a system that has
never been balanced is delivering some distribution of air that nobody has
confirmed, however carefully the ductwork was installed.

passages.title: The permit before the work
passages.text:
A confined space is not defined by how tight it is. It is defined by three
conditions taken together: the space is large enough to enter and work in, it
has limited means of entry or exit, and it is not designed for continuous
occupancy. A tank, a pit and a section of large duct can all meet that
definition, and so can places that do not look hazardous at all. The definition
turns on the difficulty of getting out, not on the discomfort of being in.

A space that meets the definition is treated as permit-required when it also
holds, or could hold, a hazardous atmosphere, or contains material that could
engulf an entrant, or has a shape that could trap someone, or presents any other
recognised serious hazard. The permit itself is not paperwork for its own sake.
It records the specific hazards identified, the steps taken to control each one,
the testing that was done and when, and the names of the people filling each
role. It is the evidence that the assessment actually happened.

Atmospheric testing follows a fixed order that reflects how quickly each hazard
kills. Oxygen is tested first, because a meter reading for anything else cannot
be trusted in an atmosphere that is oxygen-deficient or oxygen-enriched.
Flammable gases are tested next, then toxic contaminants. Testing is done from
outside the space, working downward through it, because gases stratify and a
reading at the opening says nothing about conditions at the bottom.

The role that is most often misunderstood is the attendant's. The attendant does
not enter. That is the whole point of the position: someone outside must remain
outside, maintaining contact with the entrants and able to summon rescue. An
attendant who enters to help a collapsed entrant becomes a second casualty, and
the majority of deaths in confined spaces are among would-be rescuers rather
than the original entrant.

passages.title: Reading a material list
passages.text:
A material list is not simply an inventory of what the job needs. It is a
statement of what has been counted, in a particular order, and the order carries
information that a reader who skips to the quantities will miss. Items are
grouped by system and then by size, largest first, because that is the sequence
in which material is normally set out and installed. A line that appears out of
that order is usually an addition made after the original takeoff, and is worth
a second look for exactly that reason.

Quantities appear in the unit the material is purchased in, not the unit it is
measured in on the drawing. Pipe measured in feet on a drawing may be listed in
lengths, because that is how it arrives. Fittings counted individually may be
listed by the box. A reader who treats every number as though it were the
drawing measurement will over-order in some places and under-order in others,
and the error will not be consistent enough to notice from the totals.

Allowances are the part most often misread. A list that shows a waste allowance
has already added it, and adding a further allowance on top duplicates it. A
list that shows no allowance has not, and ordering the bare figure leaves nothing
for offcuts. The only way to tell which convention is in use is to read the
heading, which is why the heading is not decoration.

None of this makes a material list difficult. It makes it a document with
conventions, like a drawing. The reader who learns the conventions can check a
list against a drawing quickly and find the discrepancies that matter. The
reader who treats it as a shopping list will order confidently and be wrong.

distractorNotes: subtracted the last piece instead of adding it
added the numerators and the denominators straight across
dropped the smallest piece when adding

questions.stem: How many 2 1/2-foot pieces can be cut from a 100-foot length, ignoring waste?
questions.explanation: Divide the total by the piece length: 100 ÷ 2.5 = 40 pieces.
distractorNotes: multiplied instead of divided
rounded the piece length down to 2 feet
rounded the piece length up to 3 feet

questions.stem: A crew of 12 works an 8-hour shift, but 3 of them leave for the whole shift. How many worker-hours are actually put in?
questions.explanation: Nine workers each put in 8 hours, giving 72 worker-hours.
distractorNotes: added an extra worker's shift
counted the full crew
counted only the workers who left

questions.stem: A part costing $85 is sold with a 20% markup. What is the selling price?
questions.explanation: A 20% markup adds 0.20 × 85 = $17 to the cost, giving $102.
distractorNotes: gave the markup amount instead of the selling price
subtracted the markup instead of adding it
added 20 dollars instead of 20 percent

questions.stem: A machine produces a part every 45 seconds. How many parts does it produce in 3 minutes?
questions.explanation: Three minutes is 180 seconds, and 180 ÷ 45 = 4 parts.
distractorNotes: multiplied instead of dividing
divided the minutes by the seconds without converting
used 30 seconds per part instead of 45

questions.stem: According to the passage, a higher gauge number means the metal is
choices: heavier per square foot
thicker
thinner
denser
questions.explanation: The passage states directly that the larger the gauge number, the thinner the metal.
distractorNotes: weight per area falls as the sheet gets thinner
reverses the relationship the passage states in its first sentence

questions.stem: The passage explains that the gauge convention originally recorded
choices: the number of sheets packed into one standard bundle
the weight in pounds of one standard sheet of the stock
how many passes through dies the metal had been through
the finished thickness measured in thousandths of an inch
questions.explanation: The passage says the number recorded how many passes the metal had been drawn through, and that more passes meant thinner stock.
distractorNotes: the passage never mentions bundling
weight per area is what a gauge refers to now, not what the number originally counted
the passage contrasts gauge numbers with decimal thickness

questions.stem: Based on the passage, ordering “sixteen gauge” without naming the material is a problem because
choices: the same gauge number is a different thickness in each metal
sixteen gauge stock is too thin to be used for most fabrication
gauge numbers have been withdrawn and no supplier still quotes them
aluminum is never ordered by gauge number under any circumstances
questions.explanation: The passage says a gauge number refers to weight per unit area, and because metals differ in density the same number is a different thickness in each.
distractorNotes: the passage makes no claim about what thickness is suitable
the passage says specifications often give gauge alongside a decimal
the passage gives sixteen gauge aluminum as an example

questions.stem: Where a drawing gives both a gauge number and a decimal thickness that disagree, the passage says
choices: the gauge number governs
the decimal thickness governs
the job must stop until the drawing is reissued
either may be used, at the fabricator's discretion
questions.explanation: The passage says the decimal governs, because it is the measurement that can be checked directly with a micrometer.
distractorNotes: reverses what the passage states
the passage gives a rule for resolving it, not a reason to stop
the passage names one of them as governing

questions.stem: The final paragraph is included mainly to
choices: show that repair work is more profitable for a shop than new work
argue that drawings more than a few years old should be destroyed
explain in detail how a micrometer is calibrated and read on sheet
warn that repair work may involve an older gauge table, so the material should be measured
questions.explanation: The paragraph says existing material may have been ordered under a table no longer in use, and that measuring the old sheet settles the question.
distractorNotes: the passage makes no comparison of that kind
the passage recommends measuring, not discarding drawings
the tool is mentioned but not explained

questions.stem: Which best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Torque wrenches are too unreliable to be trusted and should be replaced by direct measurement of stretch
A joint holds by the tension in a stretched bolt, and torque aims at that stretch indirectly
Using bolts of a higher strength grade is the surest way to make a joint hold
Over-tightening a fastener is always more damaging to a joint than under-tightening it
questions.explanation: The passage argues that clamping comes from bolt stretch, that torque aims at that stretch indirectly, and that both practices at the end exist to preserve it.
distractorNotes: the passage recommends checking them, not abandoning them
the passage opens by denying that strength is what makes the joint hold
the passage describes two different failure modes without ranking them

questions.stem: According to the passage, much of the torque applied at the wrench is consumed by
choices: friction under the nut face and in the threads
stretching the bolt, which is what produces the clamping force
bending the parts being clamped against one another
heat absorbed by the wrench and the operator's arm
questions.explanation: The passage states that a large share is consumed by friction under the nut face and in the threads, with only the remainder stretching the fastener.
distractorNotes: that is the remainder, after friction takes its share
the passage does not mention bending
the passage does not mention the wrench absorbing effort

questions.stem: The passage implies that applying the same torque figure to a dry joint and an oiled joint will
choices: produce more clamping force on the dry joint than the oiled one
produce the same clamping force on both joints
strip the threads on the oiled joint as it is tightened
produce different clamping forces
questions.explanation: The passage says the split between friction and stretch depends on the condition of the parts, so the same torque gives different clamping forces.
distractorNotes: picks a direction the passage never states; it says only that the forces differ
contradicts the passage's point about lubrication condition
the passage does not describe this outcome

questions.stem: The passage says a joint that is too loose fails because
choices: the bolt yields during assembly and no longer springs back to clamp
repeated movement between the parts works the fastener loose or fatigues it
the exposed threads corrode far more quickly than they otherwise would
the clamping force was never applied to the joint in the first place

distractorNotes: that is how the over-tightened joint fails
corrosion is not mentioned
the passage describes a joint under some clamp, just too little

questions.stem: According to the passage, the over-tightened joint differs from the loose one in that
choices: It always takes longer to fail than an under-tightened joint does
It gives no audible or visible warning of any kind while it is failing
It may already have lost its clamp before the assembly leaves the bench
It cannot be detected by any instrument available on a job site
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the loose joint, which announces itself gradually, with the over-tightened one, which may have already lost its clamp on the bench.
distractorNotes: the passage suggests the opposite timing
the passage does not discuss noise
the passage does not claim this

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about

how to design a duct system from scratch for a new building
why duct drawings are usually wrong and have to be reissued
how to choose a fan of the right capacity for a given building

the passage explicitly denies the design was wrong

reduces the air at that outlet and leaves the others unchanged
reduces the total air the fan delivers to zero
has no effect until every damper is closed

questions.stem: The passage suggests that balancing one outlet at a time and moving on is ineffective because

dampers wear out quickly if they are adjusted repeatedly
the fan cannot respond quickly enough to each adjustment

wear is not mentioned
fan response time is not discussed

questions.stem: When readings disagree between passes by more than a small margin, the passage says the usual cause is
choices: a damper that has slipped out of its set position
a real change somewhere in the system itself
an instrument that has drifted out of calibration
the position the measurement was taken from
questions.explanation: The passage states that where readings disagree from pass to pass, the usual cause is the measurement position rather than a change in the system.
distractorNotes: the passage does not offer this explanation
the passage names this as the less likely explanation
instrument faults are not mentioned

questions.stem: As used in the final paragraph, “reconciles” most nearly means
choices: replaces with something better
apologises for
brings into agreement
keeps separate records of
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts what a design predicts with how a system behaves, and names balancing as the step that brings the two together.
distractorNotes: balancing adjusts the system, it does not replace the design
the word is used of two things being matched, not of regret
the sentence is about closing a gap, not recording one

questions.stem: According to the passage, a confined space is defined by
choices: how physically tight and uncomfortable the space is to work in
three conditions taken together, one of which is limited entry or exit
whether the space contains, or could contain, a hazardous atmosphere
whether a permit has already been issued and signed for the space
questions.explanation: The passage lists exactly those three conditions taken together, and says the definition turns on the difficulty of getting out.
distractorNotes: the passage opens by denying this

questions.stem: The passage says oxygen is tested first because
choices: readings for other hazards cannot be trusted when oxygen is out of range
oxygen deficiency is by far the most common hazard found in such spaces
oxygen meters take the longest of the three to settle to a stable reading
the permit requires that order so the record reads consistently
questions.explanation: The passage states that a meter reading for anything else cannot be trusted in an atmosphere that is oxygen-deficient or oxygen-enriched.
distractorNotes: the passage gives a different reason
timing of the instrument is not mentioned

questions.stem: Testing is done working downward through the space because
choices: the entrant will be doing the work at the bottom of the space
the meter gives a more accurate reading when it is lowered slowly
gases settle at different levels within the space

questions.explanation: The passage says gases stratify and a reading at the opening says nothing about conditions at the bottom.

meter accuracy is not the stated reason

questions.stem: The passage says the attendant's defining responsibility is to

remain outside the space while staying in contact and able to summon rescue
complete and sign the permit paperwork before work begins
carry out the atmospheric testing before anyone goes in
questions.explanation: The passage says the attendant does not enter, and that the whole point of the position is that someone outside stays outside.
distractorNotes: the passage states the attendant does not enter
the permit records the assessment but is not named as the attendant's role

questions.stem: The last sentence is included to show that

rescue teams are generally too poorly trained for confined space work
confined space work should be avoided entirely wherever it is possible
the original entrant is rarely the one in any real danger
questions.explanation: The sentence follows the statement that an attendant who enters becomes a second casualty, and reports that most deaths are among would-be rescuers.
distractorNotes: the passage makes no claim about training
the passage describes how to do it safely

questions.stem: The passage is chiefly concerned with

how to calculate a waste allowance for a given quantity of material
why material lists ought to be replaced altogether by a set of marked-up drawings

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a line appearing out of the usual order deserves attention because

it has probably been priced incorrectly
it indicates that the list has been tampered with

whichever unit happens to be shortest to write
